incentives.question: Is the PTC still relevant in 2026, after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act?
incentives.answer: Yes, for nuclear specifically. The OBBBA (signed July 2025) terminated the tech-neutral §45Y/§48E credits early for wind and solar but kept them for nuclear: a nuclear plant qualifies if construction begins before 2034, with a three-year phase-out after that. The deployments this site tracks target operation between 2028 and 2030, comfortably inside that window; most rows publish no construction date, so start-of-construction timing is an open item per project.

points.fact: §45Y/§48E survive for new nuclear that begins construction before 2034, then phase out over three years; the emissions-based sunset trigger was replaced by these fixed dates.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives (July 2025)

points.fact: New 10% credit adder for facilities in “nuclear energy communities” (metro areas with ≥0.17% direct nuclear employment since 2010), §45Y only.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

points.fact: New risk: foreign-entity-of-concern (FEOC) restrictions apply from 2026: material-assistance thresholds on the supply chain that a HALEU/TRISO vendor has to clear to keep the credit.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

points.fact: Credit transferability (§6418) survives, except transfers to specified foreign entities; advanced nuclear companies also gain master-limited-partnership eligibility from 2026.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

displaced_alternatives.note: These grids run on diesel. The Regulatory Commission of Alaska's FY2024 Power Cost Equalization order is the definitive price sheet: its per-utility appendix gives total power cost per kWh for every participating rural utility, running from about $0.41/kWh at wind-equipped Kotzebue to $1.95/kWh at Lime Village, with fuel alone between $0.19 and $1.53/kWh. reading: Where the bands overlap is what matters. Against **rural Alaska** ($300–800+/MWh, diesel-fired, and commercial loads get no PCE subsidy) even the **FOAK band** ($140–410) wins across most of the range. That is the one uncontested market, and it is why Fort Wainwright is the most interesting row in the Army Janus table. Against **remote diesel** generally ($250–400) the FOAK band overlaps: a first unit at the top of its range ($410) loses to diesel at the bottom of its range ($250), so 'cheaper than diesel' is a site-by-site claim that turns on local fuel logistics until NOAK costs ($90–330) arrive. Against grid-connected U.S. industrial power the microreactor loses in every published case except the PTC-supported optimization ($48–78), which is forward-looking and U.S.-only. So the commercial logic flips by sector: off-grid sites can buy on cost today, while on-grid sites buy on resilience, speed-to-power or carbon and pay a premium for it.
